example_sentences.en: I am from Turkey.
Where is the nearest stop?

cloze.de: Wir ___ seit zwei Wochen in Berlin.
cloze.en: We have been in Berlin for two weeks.

words.notes: The most irregular verb in German. Its own Perfekt uses sein: 'ich bin gewesen'. In spoken German the Präteritum 'war' is used far more than the Perfekt.

example_sentences.en: I have an appointment tomorrow.
Do you have a moment?

cloze.en: Unfortunately we don't have any sugar left.

words.notes: Also the auxiliary for most Perfekt forms: 'ich habe gearbeitet'. Note the missing -b- in 'du hast' and 'er hat'.
words.germany_context: 'Haben Sie einen Termin?' is the first question at almost any German office, doctor or bank. Walk-ins are rarely accepted.

example_sentences.en: It is slowly getting cold outside.
My brother is becoming an engineer.

cloze.en: Next month I turn thirty.

words.notes: Three jobs: 'become', the future tense (ich werde arbeiten) and the passive (das wird gemacht). Takes sein in the Perfekt.

example_sentences.en: I have to work longer today.
We have to get up at seven.

cloze.de: Du ___ dich innerhalb von 14 Tagen anmelden.
cloze.en: You have to register within 14 days.

words.notes: 'nicht müssen' means 'don't have to'. For 'must not' use 'nicht dürfen'.
words.germany_context: You must do the Anmeldung at the Bürgeramt within 14 days of moving into a flat. The Anmeldebestätigung is needed for a bank account, a phone contract and your tax ID.

example_sentences.en: What did you just say?
Please tell me your address.

cloze.en: Unfortunately the boss says nothing about it.

words.notes: The person you tell goes in the dative: 'Ich sage dir das.' Use 'erzählen' for stories, 'sagen' for facts.
words.germany_context: Say 'Sie' to strangers, officials and new colleagues. The 'du' is offered by the older or more senior person first.

example_sentences.en: What are you doing at the weekend?
I'm doing a German course at the moment.

cloze.de: Können wir für Montag einen Termin ___?
cloze.en: Can we make an appointment for Monday?

words.notes: The all-purpose verb: 'Essen machen', 'Urlaub machen', 'Das macht 5 Euro' (that comes to 5 euros). 'Mach's gut!' = take care.
words.germany_context: Almost everything here runs on appointments. 'einen Termin machen' applies to the doctor, the Bürgeramt, the bank and even some hairdressers.

example_sentences.en: Pass me the salt, please.

example_sentences.de: Es gibt hier viele gute Bäckereien.
example_sentences.en: There are a lot of good bakeries here.

cloze.de: Ich ___ dir morgen das Geld zurück.
cloze.en: I'll give you the money back tomorrow.

words.notes: 'es gibt' + accusative = 'there is / there are' and is used constantly. Person in the dative, thing in the accusative.
words.germany_context: Tips are given directly to the waiter when you pay: round up 5–10 % and say the total out loud. Leaving coins on the table is unusual.

example_sentences.en: I come from Turkey.
When does the next bus come?

cloze.de: Meine Freunde ___ heute Abend zu uns.
cloze.en: My friends are coming to our place tonight.

words.notes: Movement verb, so the Perfekt takes sein: 'ich bin gekommen'. 'Woher kommen Sie?' is the standard way to ask where someone is from.
words.germany_context: Punctuality is taken literally: coming at 18:00 means 18:00, and being five minutes late already deserves a quick message.

example_sentences.de: Ich gehe jeden Morgen zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
example_sentences.en: I walk to work every morning.
How are you?

cloze.en: We're going to the cinema tonight.

words.notes: Means going on foot; for vehicles use 'fahren'. 'Das geht (nicht)' = that works / that doesn't work.
words.germany_context: Pedestrians wait for the green man even on an empty street. Crossing at red is frowned upon and can cost a small fine.

example_sentences.en: Unfortunately I don't know.

example_sentences.de: Weißt du, wo der Bahnhof ist?
example_sentences.en: Do you know where the station is?

cloze.en: He knows the answer exactly.

words.notes: 'wissen' = know a fact; 'kennen' = be familiar with a person, place or thing. Watch the ß in ich/du/er.
words.mnemonic: weiß like 'wise' — a wise person knows.

example_sentences.de: Ich sehe dich morgen im Büro.
example_sentences.en: I'll see you at the office tomorrow.

example_sentences.de: Siehst du das rote Haus dort?
example_sentences.en: Do you see the red house over there?

cloze.en: We're watching a film at the weekend.

words.notes: e→ie in du and er. 'Wir sehen uns!' is a normal casual goodbye.

example_sentences.de: Lass mich bitte kurz in Ruhe.
example_sentences.en: Please leave me alone for a moment.

example_sentences.de: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad heute zu Hause.
example_sentences.en: I'm leaving my bike at home today.

cloze.de: Er ___ sein Auto in der Werkstatt reparieren.
cloze.en: He's having his car repaired at the garage.

words.notes: Three uses: leave something somewhere, let someone do something, and have something done by someone else. 'Lass uns gehen!' = let's go.

example_sentences.en: I'm standing in front of the supermarket.

example_sentences.de: Die Flaschen stehen in der Küche.
example_sentences.en: The bottles are in the kitchen.

cloze.de: Wir ___ seit zwanzig Minuten in der Schlange.
cloze.en: We've been standing in the queue for twenty minutes.

words.notes: For upright objects German says 'stehen', not 'sein'. 'stellen' is the active counterpart: to put something upright.
words.germany_context: On escalators in stations, stand on the right and keep the left side free for people walking up.

example_sentences.en: I can't find my key.
What do you think of the flat?

cloze.de: Er ___ seine neue Arbeit sehr interessant.
cloze.en: He finds his new job very interesting.

words.notes: 'Ich finde das gut' means 'I think that's good' — the everyday way to give an opinion.
words.germany_context: Finding a flat in a big city means a Besichtigung with 30 other people, plus a SCHUFA credit report and three payslips ready as a PDF.

example_sentences.en: I'm staying at home today.

example_sentences.de: Wie lange bleibst du in Deutschland?
example_sentences.en: How long are you staying in Germany?

cloze.de: Wir ___ noch eine Woche in München.
cloze.en: We're staying in Munich for another week.

words.notes: One of the few non-movement verbs with sein in the Perfekt: 'ich bin geblieben'. 'Bleib gesund!' is a common goodbye.

example_sentences.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
example_sentences.en: The book is lying on the table.
Cologne is on the Rhine.

cloze.en: My keys are in the hallway.

words.notes: 'liegen' = to lie (position, no movement); 'legen' = to lay something down. Also used for towns: 'Berlin liegt im Osten.'

example_sentences.en: My name is Emre.
What's your name?

cloze.en: My colleague's name is Anna.

words.notes: The normal way to give your name — not 'mein Name ist', which sounds formal. 'Was heißt das auf Deutsch?' = what does that mean in German?

example_sentences.de: Ich denke oft an meine Familie.
example_sentences.en: I often think about my family.
What do you think about it?

cloze.de: Sie ___, dass das eine gute Idee ist.
cloze.en: She thinks that's a good idea.

words.notes: 'denken an' + accusative = think about someone or something. Mixed verb: regular endings but vowel change in the past (dachte, gedacht).

example_sentences.de: Ich nehme den Bus zur Arbeit.
example_sentences.en: I take the bus to work.

example_sentences.de: Nimm bitte noch ein Stück Kuchen.
example_sentences.en: Please take another piece of cake.

cloze.en: Do you take sugar in your coffee?

words.notes: Strong irregular: du nimmst, er nimmt (double m, no h). 'Ich nehme das' is how you order in a café or shop.
words.mnemonic: nimm! ~ 'nim' as in nimble hands taking something.

example_sentences.en: What should I do now?
My back hurts.

cloze.en: He does nothing all day.

words.notes: In everyday speech 'machen' replaces 'tun' most of the time. The big exception is 'weh tun' (to hurt), which you will need at the doctor.

example_sentences.en: I think that's right.
Do you believe me?

cloze.de: Sie ___, dass der Zug Verspätung hat.
cloze.en: She thinks the train is delayed.

words.notes: The person you believe goes in the dative: 'Ich glaube dir.' 'Ich glaube' is the everyday softener for an opinion.

example_sentences.de: Kannst du kurz meine Tasche halten?
example_sentences.en: Can you hold my bag for a second?
The train stops in Frankfurt.

cloze.de: Der Bus ___ nicht an dieser Haltestelle.
cloze.en: The bus doesn't stop at this stop.

words.notes: Both 'hold' and 'stop' (for vehicles) — hence 'die Haltestelle', the stop. 'Was hältst du davon?' = what do you think of it?

example_sentences.en: Everyone calls him Max.

example_sentences.de: Können Sie mir einen Preis nennen?
example_sentences.en: Can you give me a price?

cloze.en: What do you call that in German?

words.notes: Mixed verb like 'kennen': nannte, genannt. 'nennen' = give a name to something; 'heißen' = to be called.

example_sentences.de: Zeigen Sie mir bitte Ihren Ausweis.
example_sentences.en: Please show me your ID.

example_sentences.de: Ich zeige dir am Wochenende die Stadt.
example_sentences.en: I'll show you the city at the weekend.

cloze.de: Sie ___ uns Fotos von ihrer Reise.
cloze.en: She shows us photos from her trip.

words.notes: Person in the dative, thing in the accusative — same pattern as 'geben'.
words.germany_context: Ticket inspectors on the U-Bahn and buses are usually in plain clothes. Show a valid ticket or pay a 60 € Erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt on the spot.

example_sentences.en: This street leads to the station.

example_sentences.de: Meine Nachbarin führt ein kleines Café.
example_sentences.en: My neighbour runs a small café.

cloze.en: The path leads straight to the lake.

words.notes: Used for roads and paths, for running a business, and for 'ein Gespräch führen' (to have a conversation).

example_sentences.en: Do you speak English?

example_sentences.de: Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch.
example_sentences.en: I only speak a little German.

cloze.en: Unfortunately my colleague speaks very fast.

words.notes: e→i in du and er. 'Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?' is the sentence you will use most in your first months.
words.germany_context: Most Behörden work in German only. The Volkshochschule Integrationskurs is the standard, heavily subsidised route to B1.

example_sentences.de: Ich bringe dir einen Kaffee mit.
example_sentences.en: I'll bring you a coffee.

example_sentences.de: Bringst du das Paket zur Post?
example_sentences.en: Are you taking the parcel to the post office?

cloze.en: The waiter will bring the bill in a moment.

words.notes: Mixed verb: brachte, gebracht. Unlike English, 'bringen' also covers taking something to a place.

example_sentences.de: Ich lebe seit einem Jahr in Deutschland.
example_sentences.en: I've been living in Germany for a year.
My parents live in Izmir.

cloze.en: We like living in this city.

words.notes: 'leben' = to be alive or live in a country in general; 'wohnen' = to reside at a concrete address.

example_sentences.de: Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Hamburg.
example_sentences.en: I'm going to Hamburg by train.
Do you drive?

cloze.en: The bus runs every ten minutes.

words.notes: a→ä in du and er. Perfekt with sein for the journey ('ich bin gefahren'), with haben when you drive a vehicle as an object ('ich habe das Auto gefahren').
words.germany_context: The Deutschlandticket is a monthly subscription covering all regional trains, buses, trams and U-Bahn across the whole country — usually the cheapest way to get around.

example_sentences.en: What do you mean by that?

example_sentences.de: Ich meine den Mann dort vorne.
example_sentences.en: I mean the man over there.

cloze.en: She thinks we should leave earlier.

words.notes: 'Wie meinen Sie das?' is the polite way to ask someone to explain. For word meanings use 'bedeuten' or 'heißen', not 'meinen'.

example_sentences.en: I'll ask the caretaker.
May I ask you something?

cloze.en: He always asks for directions.

words.notes: The person asked takes the accusative: 'Ich frage dich.' 'fragen nach' = to ask for or about something.

example_sentences.en: I don't know this street.
Do you know my colleague?

cloze.de: Wir ___ ein gutes Restaurant in der Nähe.
cloze.en: We know a good restaurant nearby.

words.notes: 'kennen' takes a direct object (a person, place, thing). 'wissen' takes facts and clauses: 'Ich weiß, dass …'.
words.mnemonic: kennen ~ 'to be acquainted' (cf. 'ken' in Scottish English).

example_sentences.en: I work as a software developer.
Do you work on Friday too?

cloze.en: My wife often works from home.

words.notes: Stem ends in -t, so an extra -e- appears: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. 'arbeiten bei' + company, 'arbeiten als' + job title.
words.germany_context: Full-time is usually 38–40 hours. By law you get at least 20 paid holidays on a five-day week, and Feierabend is taken seriously: after hours, people stop answering messages.

example_sentences.de: Ich brauche einen Termin beim Arzt.
example_sentences.en: I need an appointment at the doctor's.
Do you need help?

cloze.de: Für die Anmeldung ___ man einen Pass.
cloze.en: You need a passport for the registration.

words.notes: Takes the accusative. Careful with 'brauchen' vs 'gebrauchen'; and 'du brauchst nicht zu kommen' = you don't need to come.
words.germany_context: For the Anmeldung you need your passport, the filled-in form and a Wohnungsgeberbestätigung signed by your landlord. Without the landlord's form the appointment is wasted.

example_sentences.en: Please follow me.

example_sentences.de: Der Hund folgt seinem Herrchen überall hin.
example_sentences.en: The dog follows its owner everywhere.

cloze.en: I follow you on Instagram.

words.notes: Dative verb: 'Ich folge dir', never 'dich'. Movement, so the Perfekt takes sein.

example_sentences.de: Ich lerne jeden Tag zwanzig neue Wörter.
example_sentences.en: I learn twenty new words every day.
Where did you learn German?

cloze.de: Meine Tochter ___ seit einem Jahr Klavier.
cloze.en: My daughter has been learning piano for a year.

words.notes: 'lernen' = learn or study for school; 'studieren' means specifically to be at university.
words.germany_context: Every town has a Volkshochschule with cheap evening German courses, and new residents can often get a subsidised Integrationskurs through the BAMF.

example_sentences.en: I passed the exam.

example_sentences.de: Unser Team besteht aus fünf Leuten.
example_sentences.en: Our team consists of five people.

cloze.en: He'll definitely pass the test.

words.notes: 'eine Prüfung bestehen' = pass an exam; 'bestehen aus' = consist of; 'bestehen auf' = insist on. No ge- in the participle: bestanden.
words.germany_context: For citizenship you must pass the 'Leben in Deutschland' test — 33 multiple-choice questions on law, history and everyday rules.

example_sentences.en: I'm afraid I don't understand you.
Do you understand this word?

cloze.en: On the phone I understand almost nothing.

words.notes: No ge- in the participle: verstanden. Pair it with 'Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?' — the most useful follow-up you will own.

example_sentences.en: Please have a seat.

example_sentences.de: Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl.
example_sentences.en: I'm putting the child on the chair.

cloze.de: Wir ___ uns an den Tisch am Fenster.
cloze.en: We sit down at the table by the window.

words.notes: Mostly used reflexively: 'sich setzen' = to sit down (the movement); 'sitzen' = to be sitting (the state).

example_sentences.de: Ich bekomme jeden Monat eine Rechnung.
example_sentences.en: I get a bill every month.
Did you get my message?

cloze.de: Wann ___ ich eine Antwort vom Amt?
cloze.en: When do I get an answer from the office?

words.notes: Classic false friend: 'bekommen' = to receive, NOT 'to become' (that is 'werden'). No ge- in the participle: bekommen.
words.mnemonic: Do not 'become' a steak — you 'bekommen' one.
words.germany_context: After the Anmeldung your Steuer-ID arrives by post within about two weeks. Your employer needs it, otherwise you are taxed at the highest class.

example_sentences.en: The German course begins in September.
When does the film start?

cloze.de: Die Arbeit ___ jeden Tag um acht.
cloze.en: Work starts at eight every day.

words.notes: 'anfangen' is the more colloquial synonym and is separable: 'Der Film fängt an.' No ge- in begonnen.

example_sentences.en: Tell me about your day.

example_sentences.de: Meine Oma erzählt gern alte Geschichten.
example_sentences.en: My grandma likes telling old stories.

cloze.en: He always tells us the same thing.

words.notes: 'erzählen' = tell a story or recount events; 'sagen' = state a fact. Person in the dative. No ge- in erzählt.

example_sentences.de: Ich versuche es später noch einmal.
example_sentences.en: I'll try again later.
Try this cheese!

cloze.de: Wir ___, online einen Termin zu bekommen.
cloze.en: We're trying to get an appointment online.

words.notes: Followed by 'zu' + infinitive: 'Ich versuche zu schlafen.' No ge- in versucht.

example_sentences.de: Ich schreibe dir gleich eine E-Mail.
example_sentences.en: I'll write you an email right away.
How do you spell that?

cloze.de: Sie ___ jeden Morgen eine kurze Nachricht.
cloze.en: She writes a short message every morning.

words.notes: 'Wie schreibt man das?' is how you ask for a spelling. Perfekt: hat geschrieben.
words.germany_context: Cancelling a contract — gym, phone, flat — usually has to be schriftlich, often as a signed letter by post, and with a notice period of one to three months.

example_sentences.de: Ich laufe jeden Morgen im Park.
example_sentences.en: I run in the park every morning.

example_sentences.de: Der Film läuft schon seit zehn Minuten.
example_sentences.en: The film has been running for ten minutes.

cloze.de: Wir ___ heute zu Fuß nach Hause.
cloze.en: We're walking home today.

words.notes: Means 'run', but in everyday speech also simply 'walk'. Also used for machines and films: 'Die Waschmaschine läuft.'

example_sentences.de: Ich esse gern Brot mit Käse.
example_sentences.en: I like eating bread with cheese.
What do you eat for breakfast?

cloze.en: We're eating at a restaurant tonight.

words.notes: du and er share the same form: isst. Participle is irregular: gegessen. 'Guten Appetit!' is said before every meal.
words.germany_context: Tip by rounding up 5–10 % and telling the waiter the total when you pay. 'Stimmt so' means keep the change. Card payment is normal now, but small places may still be cash only.

example_sentences.de: Ich trinke morgens immer einen Kaffee.
example_sentences.en: I always drink a coffee in the morning.
What would you like to drink?

cloze.en: In the evening he likes to drink tea.

words.notes: Regular endings, irregular stem in the past: trank, getrunken.
words.germany_context: Nearly all bottles and cans carry Pfand (8–25 cents). Take the empties back to the machine in any supermarket and you get the money back as a voucher.

example_sentences.en: I usually sleep seven hours.
Are you asleep already?

cloze.en: The child is still asleep.

words.notes: a→ä in du and er. 'Schlaf gut!' = sleep well. 'einschlafen' (separable) = to fall asleep.
words.germany_context: Nachtruhe runs from 22:00 to 06:00: no vacuuming, no loud music, no moving furniture. In an Altbau the neighbours hear everything.

example_sentences.de: Ich lese jeden Abend ein bisschen.
example_sentences.en: I read a bit every evening.

example_sentences.de: Liest du die Nachrichten auf Deutsch?
example_sentences.en: Do you read the news in German?

cloze.en: He reads the contract very carefully.

words.notes: e→ie: du liest, er liest — both the same because the stem already ends in -s. Imperative: lies!
words.germany_context: Read the Mietvertrag before signing: it fixes the Kaution (up to three months' cold rent), the notice period and how the Nebenkosten are settled once a year.

example_sentences.en: The children are playing in the courtyard.
Do you play football?

cloze.en: We often play cards on Sunday.

words.notes: Used for sports, games and instruments: 'Klavier spielen', 'Fußball spielen'.

example_sentences.de: Ich kaufe mein Brot immer beim Bäcker.
example_sentences.en: I always buy my bread at the bakery.
Where do you buy your vegetables?

cloze.en: She's buying herself a new bike.

words.notes: 'einkaufen' (separable) means to do the shopping in general: 'Ich kaufe samstags ein.'
words.germany_context: Supermarkets close around 20:00 and are shut all day Sunday and on public holidays. Do the big shop on Saturday, or you are left with a Späti or the station shop.

example_sentences.en: I live in Berlin-Neukölln.
Where exactly do you live?

cloze.de: Meine Eltern ___ in einer kleinen Wohnung.
cloze.en: My parents live in a small flat.

words.notes: 'wohnen' = live at an address; 'leben' = be alive or live in a country generally. 'wohnen in' + Dativ, 'wohnen bei' + person.
words.germany_context: Wherever you live, you must do the Anmeldung at the Bürgeramt within 14 days. Without the Anmeldebestätigung there is no bank account, no tax ID and no residence permit.

example_sentences.en: I like listening to Turkish music.
Can you hear me?

cloze.en: The neighbour listens to loud music at night.

words.notes: One verb for both 'hear' and 'listen'. 'zuhören' (separable, + Dativ) means to listen attentively to someone.
words.germany_context: Keep music at Zimmerlautstärke after 22:00. In German flats the walls are thin and a Beschwerde from a neighbour can end up with the Hausverwaltung.

example_sentences.de: Ich warte an der Haltestelle auf den Bus.
example_sentences.en: I'm waiting for the bus at the stop.
Have you been waiting long?

cloze.de: Wir ___ seit einer Stunde auf den Arzt.
cloze.en: We've been waiting for the doctor for an hour.

words.notes: 'warten auf' + Akkusativ. Stem ends in -t, so du wartest, er wartet.
words.germany_context: Bürgeramt appointments are often booked out for weeks. Check the online calendar very early in the morning — cancelled slots reappear then.

example_sentences.en: Can you help me, please?

example_sentences.de: Ich helfe dir gern beim Umzug.
example_sentences.en: I'm happy to help you with the move.

cloze.de: Der Hausmeister ___ uns bei der Heizung.
cloze.en: The caretaker helps us with the heating.

words.notes: Dative verb: 'Ich helfe dir', never 'dich'. e→i in du and er. 'helfen bei' + Dativ for the task.
words.germany_context: Every apartment block has a Hausmeister — the person to contact for a broken heater, a blocked drain or a lost cellar key, not the landlord directly.

example_sentences.de: Ich danke Ihnen für die Hilfe.
example_sentences.en: Thank you for your help.
We thank you warmly.

cloze.de: Er ___ seiner Kollegin für den Tipp.
cloze.en: He thanks his colleague for the tip.

words.notes: Dative for the person, 'für' + Akkusativ for the thing. In speech plain 'Danke' or 'Vielen Dank' is far more common than the full verb.

example_sentences.en: I really like the flat.
Do you like the city?

cloze.en: All of us like the new office.

words.notes: Works backwards from English: the thing liked is the subject, the person goes in the dative. No ge- in the participle: gefallen.
words.mnemonic: 'Es gefällt mir' — literally 'it is pleasing to me'.

example_sentences.en: The bike belongs to me.
Whose bag is this?

cloze.en: Waste glass belongs in the glass container.

words.notes: Dative verb: 'Das gehört mir.' With 'in' + Akkusativ it means where something should go.
words.germany_context: Mülltrennung is compulsory: Papier, Bio, Restmüll, Gelber Sack, and glass sorted by colour. Glass containers may only be used between 07:00 and 20:00 and never on Sunday.

example_sentences.en: What happened here?
That sort of thing often happens to me.

cloze.de: Auf der Autobahn ___ jeden Tag Unfälle.
cloze.en: Accidents happen on the motorway every day.

words.notes: Change-of-state verb, so the Perfekt takes sein: 'Es ist passiert.' No ge- in the participle. The person affected goes in the dative.
words.germany_context: In an emergency call 112 for ambulance and fire or 110 for the police. Both are free from any phone, and the operators usually speak English.

example_sentences.de: Ich treffe meine Freunde am Samstag.
example_sentences.en: I'm meeting my friends on Saturday.
Where are we meeting?

cloze.de: Er ___ seinen Chef morgen um zehn.
cloze.en: He's meeting his boss tomorrow at ten.

words.notes: e→i in du and er. Reflexive 'sich treffen mit' = to meet up with someone. 'eine Entscheidung treffen' = to make a decision.

example_sentences.en: I've lost my key.
Do you often lose your things?

cloze.en: Unfortunately our team loses every game.

words.notes: Irregular past: verlor, verloren — no ge- because of the ver- prefix.
words.germany_context: Every city has a Fundbüro for lost property, and items left on buses or trains go to the transport operator's own office first. Report a lost ID card to the police.

example_sentences.en: Our team almost always wins.
She won a prize.

cloze.en: Who is winning the game tonight?

words.notes: Past forms change the vowel twice: gewann, gewonnen. The ge- is part of the stem, so there is no extra ge- in the participle.

example_sentences.de: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
example_sentences.en: Could you open the window, please?

example_sentences.de: Die Bank öffnet um neun Uhr.
example_sentences.en: The bank opens at nine.

cloze.en: I'll open the door for you.

words.notes: 'aufmachen' is the everyday spoken version. A sign saying 'geöffnet' means open.
words.germany_context: Öffnungszeiten are strict: most shops run 08:00–20:00 Monday to Saturday and stay shut on Sundays and public holidays. Bakeries at stations are the usual exception.

example_sentences.en: Please close the door.
The shop closes at eight.

cloze.de: Die Apotheke ___ heute schon um 18 Uhr.
cloze.en: The pharmacy closes at 6 p.m. today.

words.notes: 'zumachen' is the colloquial version. A sign saying 'geschlossen' means closed. Note the short o in schloss, geschlossen.
words.germany_context: Sunday is the big one: supermarkets, Baumärkte and most shops are completely closed. Only stations, airports, petrol stations and Spätis stay open.

example_sentences.en: I'm carrying the heavy bags.

example_sentences.de: Sie trägt heute einen roten Mantel.
example_sentences.en: She's wearing a red coat today.

cloze.en: Can you carry the box, please?

words.notes: One verb for both 'carry' and 'wear'. a→ä in du and er: du trägst, er trägt.
